newsitem.title: USA: Sabena CEO sees loss through 1997.
newsitem.headline: Sabena CEO sees loss through 1997.

text.p: Belgian airline Sabena expects to post a loss in 1997 as well as 1996, but should break even during 1998, chief executive officer Paul Reutlinger said Friday. He declined to give figures.
"We foresee a loss in 1997 as well as 1996," he said at a news conference to unveil Cincinnati-Brussels air service which he said should improve profitability significantly.
The airline lost about two billion Belgian francs in the first half and has been expected to post a loss for the year.
"It's impossible to turn these losses around in 12 months, but we should reach a break-even point in 1998," he said.

Sabena has been hurt by strikes and protracted contract talks, as well as by the European economy and, to some extent, revenues have been hurt by the "Chunnel" Tunnel under the English Channel, Reutlinger said.
The Cincinnati service, to begin May 15, is part of a four-way partnership for management of transatlantic flights.

Sabena, Switzerland's Swissair, Austrian Airlines and Atlanta-based Delta Air Lines plan as of February 1 to coordinate fares and seating and share profits and costs. Passengers in mileage programs will also benefit.

Delta has a secondary hub at Cincinnati. With the five weekly Cincinnati-Brussels round trips it plans, Sabena will become the first non-U.S. airline to serve the Cincinnati airport, across the Ohio River in Florence,Ky.
Sabena said it will use Airbus A340-200 and -300 series aircraft, which seat 232 to 282 passengers.
Asked about a possible plan to move its pilots out of Belgium to avoid high Belgian taxes, he said Sabena hopes for an agreement by January 1998. Pilots must approve such a plan.
"Delocalizing pilots is an element that is tremendously important to get us into the profit zone," Reutlinger said.
